title: Direct Proof
short: Assume the hypothesis, rewrite it with definitions (an even number is 2k), and reason step by step to the conclusion.
trouble: Students check a few numbers and call that a proof, or write two different even numbers as 2k and 2k with the same k.

blocks.html: In geometry you wrote two-column proofs: each line a fact, each fact justified. A direct proof in discrete math is the same idea written as sentences. It chains valid steps (modus ponens, over and over), and unlike a list of examples it covers every case at once.

To prove "if $P$, then $Q$" directly: assume $P$, rewrite it using definitions, and reason step by step until you reach $Q$. Definitions turn words into algebra: $n$ is even when $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$; $n$ is odd when $n = 2k + 1$ for some integer $k$; $a$ divides $b$, written $a \mid b$, when $b = ak$ for some integer $k$.

Writing an odd number as $2k + 1$ with $k$ unknown is what makes the proof general. Every odd number has that form, so an argument that only uses the form works for all of them at once. An example like $n = 7$ uses the specific number $7$ and says nothing about $9$ or $1001$. The letter $k$ is a stand-in for "whatever it happens to be."

blocks.title: The product of two odd numbers is odd
blocks.q: Prove: if $m$ and $n$ are odd, then $mn$ is odd.
steps: Assume $m$ and $n$ are odd. Then $m = 2a + 1$ and $n = 2b + 1$ for some integers $a$ and $b$. (Two letters, because $m$ and $n$ may be different.)
Factor $2$ from the first three terms: $mn = 2(2ab + a + b) + 1$.
$2ab + a + b$ is an integer, so $mn$ has the form $2k + 1$: it is odd.

blocks.title: Divisibility is transitive
blocks.q: Prove: if $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$, then $a \mid c$.
steps: Assume $a \mid b$ and $b \mid c$. By definition, $b = ak$ and $c = bj$ for some integers $k$ and $j$.
$kj$ is an integer, so $c$ is $a$ times an integer: $a \mid c$.

blocks.title: A remainder pattern
blocks.q: Prove: if $n$ is odd, then $n^{2} - 1$ is a multiple of $4$.
steps: $k^{2} + k$ is an integer, so $n^{2} - 1$ is a multiple of $4$. (With one more idea, that $k^{2} + k = k(k + 1)$ is even, you can show it is a multiple of $8$.)

blocks.html: Checking numbers, or reusing a letter. "$3 \cdot 5 = 15$ and $7 \cdot 9 = 63$ are odd" is evidence, not a proof. And writing two even numbers as $2k$ and $2k$ quietly assumes they are equal: the "proof" that the sum of two evens is a multiple of $4$ ($2k + 2k = 4k$) fails for $2 + 4 = 6$. Check: each new number gets its own letter, and every step must hold for every value of the letters.
